limits: Chapter is a brief survey ('we briefly mention'); most claims are reported from cited work without data or setups.
Only illustrative experiment is Fig 7.1 (one Thompson-sampling run); no hyperparameters beyond arm weights, sigma^2=1 and a conjugate prior.
Author concedes LLM-based PSRL fails beyond tiny problems (fn 3).
Subgoal discovery methods rely on discrete subgoal spaces (7.5.3.1); skill chaining needs explicit goal states (7.5.1.6); option-critic works poorly under sparse reward (7.5.1.7).
Offline RL is fundamentally more limited than online RL as the agent cannot explore (7.7.4).
practices: Use Bayes-optimal methods when a prior over models is available; use regret-minimising methods when no prior can be specified or noise may be adversarial (7.1.3, Table 7.1).
Approximate Bayesian exploration with Thompson sampling: sample one parameter set from the posterior and act greedily (7.2.2.1, Eq 7.21).
For optimism, use UCB: empirical mean plus c/sqrt(N) bonus, or posterior mean plus c times posterior std (7.2.3, Eq 7.26, 7.28).
Train value functions with a cross-entropy loss on a discretised target (HL-Gauss) instead of MSE (7.3.2).
Prefer KL/information-gain intrinsic rewards or ICM-style latent prediction over raw prediction error to avoid the noisy-TV trap (7.4.1.3).
In HRL, add a deliberation cost to prevent options switching every step (7.5.1.9) and use hindsight relabeling (HIRO, HAC) to handle non-stationarity (7.5.2.4).
For offline RL constrain the learned policy near the behavior policy, penalise uncertainty, or use conservative Q-learning (7.7.1).
Prefer larger, more diverse offline datasets for better offline RL performance (7.7.1, citing Kum+23).
Use DAgger or offline-to-online finetuning to avoid compounding error of behavior cloning (7.7.4.2).
In offline model-based RL penalise reward by model uncertainty (MOPO) or send high-uncertainty transitions to an absorbing state (MOREL) (7.7.2).
